records.name_note: Many common names are in circulation for this species: NC State Extension lists "American Sweet Gum," "Redgum," "Red Sweet Gum," "Sweetgum," "Sweet Gum," and "Sweetgum Tree"; RHS separately lists "American red gum," "American sweet gum," "bilsted," "copalm balsam," "red gum," and "satin walnut." All refer to the same species, Liquidambar styraciflua -- no alternate binomial or taxonomic split is indicated by any admissible source.
unknowns: Gumball litter/underfoot hazard (decision-relevant; no dedicated schema field): NC State Extension tags this species '#messy fruits' and describes its fruit as 'Spherical, spiny fruiting heads, known as gumballs' 1 to 3 inches in diameter, noting 'fruit litters the ground between December and April.' This is a slip/puncture-underfoot and cleanup hazard distinct from toxicity -- worth surfacing for anyone considering this tree near walkways, patios, play areas, or bare feet. Clemson HGIC gives the flip side: 'the seeds within the gumballs are a very important source of food for many of our over-wintering songbirds,' so the same litter has real wildlife value. NC State separately lists a fruitless cultivar, 'Rotundiloba' (marketed as 'Fruitless Sweetgum, Thornless Sweetgum'), as an option for avoiding the gumball problem while keeping the species' fall color.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: left null. No admissible source addresses toxicity to cats or dogs (or humans) for this species. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox page -- which carries explicit 'Poison'/'Problem for cats'/'Problem for dogs' tags for many other species in this catalog -- has no Poison section and no toxicity tags at all for Liquidambar styraciflua. RHS's plant profile page (checked directly for the words toxic, poison, pets, cats, dogs, harmful) contains none of them. Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, and UGA CAES pages found for this species discuss fall color, pests, wind/hurricane resistance, and litter, never a toxic principle or animal-safety statement. Per this catalog's rule, absence of any toxicity claim is not evidence of non-toxicity, so this was left null rather than inferred false.

soil_ph_min: left null. UF/IFAS gives only an upper bound ('pH of 7 or less'); no admissible source states a lower pH bound. NC State's own structured pH tag for this page reads 'Soil pH: Acid (<6.0) Neutral (6.0-8.0)' -- this catalog has already confirmed elsewhere (e.g. the Acer rubrum and Cornus kousa records) that this exact two-category combination is generic, reused site-wide boilerplate rather than a species-curated number, so it was not used for either soil_ph bound here.

soil_drainage: left null. Admissible sources describe genuinely broad, near-opposite tolerance rather than one regime. NC State's own tags for this page span 'Good Drainage,' 'Moist,' 'Occasionally Dry,' and 'Occasionally Wet' simultaneously, and its habitat text says the tree is 'frequently found in wet river bottoms, in swamps that frequently flood, and on drier uplands.' NC State separately tags it '#drought tolerant' and states it is 'resistant to fire, heat, drought, soil compaction, deer and rabbits.' Clemson HGIC marks it (with an asterisk) among trees 'more tolerant of very wet or periodically flooded conditions.' UF/IFAS lists soil tolerances as 'wet to well-drained.' Given documented tolerance spanning flood-prone wet soil through drought resistance, no single fast/moderate/moisture_retentive category fits without discarding part of what the sources say, so this was left null, consistent with this catalog's prior treatment of Acer rubrum and Ulmus americana.

water_regime: left null for the same reason as soil_drainage. No admissible source recommends either keeping soil consistently moist or deliberately drying it down between waterings -- the sources instead describe an established landscape tree tolerating flood-prone wet sites and drought about equally, which does not cleanly match keep_moist, keep_barely_moist, dry_surface_between, or dry_thoroughly_between.

Family classification discrepancy: NC State Extension places this species in family 'Altingiaceae,' while RHS's structured Family field reads 'Hamamelidaceae.' This reflects older vs. newer (APG) taxonomic treatments of the genus Liquidambar rather than any disagreement about the species identity itself; noted here since there is no schema field for family.

Root/infrastructure placement hazard (decision-relevant, no dedicated field): UF/IFAS warns 'Be careful when locating Sweetgum as a street tree since its large, aggressive roots may lift curbs and sidewalks.'

Self-seeding/volunteer tendency (decision-relevant, no dedicated field): Clemson HGIC lists sweetgum among trees that 'can seed prolifically,' producing unwanted volunteer seedlings that may require cut-stump herbicide control in beds and lawns.

chill_damage_f / cool_rest_note: left null. No admissible source states a specific sublethal cold-damage-onset temperature. Sources give only USDA hardiness-zone survival data (NC State: zones 5a-9b; UF/IFAS: zones 5B-10A; RHS: H6, hardy to -20 to -15C) plus UF/IFAS's separate qualitative note that the tree 'leafs out early in the spring and is sometimes damage[d] by frost' -- a frost-timing caveat about new spring growth, not a stated damage-onset degree figure, so it was not mapped to chill_damage_f.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max/humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max/light_fc_min/light_fc_good: left null. These read as indoor-microclimate and container-culture fields; no admissible source discusses ambient day/night temperature, humidity, or foot-candle light levels for this outdoor landscape tree.

direct_sun_hours_max: left null. NC State's parenthetical '(6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' is that site's fixed, generic legend text defining its 'Full sun' category (confirmed reused verbatim across unrelated species pages elsewhere in this catalog), not a species-curated sun-hours ceiling, so the number 6 was not extracted as a distinct data point.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: left null. No admissible source gives any fertilizing schedule, calendar month, or dilution/strength guidance specific to Liquidambar styraciflua; none of the fetched pages (NC State, UF/IFAS, RHS, Clemson, Penn State) contain a Fertilizer section for this species.

water_check_depth_cm / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis / water_dry_down_target: left null. No admissible source frames watering as a checkable numeric schedule (soil-probe depth, day interval) for this in-ground, established landscape tree.

Missouri Botanical Garden's Liquidambar styraciflua Plant Finder page (plantfinder.mobot.org, an admissible source) could not be verified by direct fetch -- repeated attempts failed with a TLS certificate verification error, not a content issue -- so despite search-result snippets suggesting it discusses gumball litter and hardiness, it is not represented among this record's citations and was not relied on for any field.

records.name_note: Genus is frequently misspelled "Buddleia" in commerce and casual use, but "Buddleja" (silent j, honoring Rev. Adam Buddle) is the botanically correct spelling under the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature.
unknowns: Invasive/regulated status: multiple admissible sources flag Buddleja davidii as invasive or regulated in parts of the US -- NC State notes it is 'listed as invasive by the NC Invasive Plant Council in the Mountain and Piedmont regions of North Carolina' and 'listed as a severe threat by the North Carolina Native Plant Society'; Missouri Botanical Garden notes it 'has been declared a noxious weed in Oregon and Washington' and has naturalized in the eastern US, Washington, Oregon, California and Hawaii; Clemson HGIC states 'In some areas of the US, it is considered weedy, and its planting is discouraged'; University of Maryland Extension states it 'is an invasive species and spreads into natural areas by seed' and that Maryland's Department of Agriculture has it 'on a list of species prioritized for assessment in 2026' under the Maryland Prohibited Invasive Plant Law; Penn State Extension discourages its use because native caterpillars cannot feed on it and its wind-dispersed seed readily escapes cultivation. There is no dedicated schema field for this, but it is decision-relevant for a care app since some jurisdictions restrict sale/planting.

toxic_to_pets left null: none of the admissible sources fetched (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson HGIC, RHS, Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension) contain any statement addressing toxicity of Buddleja davidii to cats, dogs, or any other animal or human. Absence of a toxicity mention is not treated as evidence of non-toxicity per the task rules, so both toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than inferred either way.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, and direct_sun_hours_max are left null: this species is described exclusively by the admissible sources as a cold-hardy, in-ground outdoor garden shrub (USDA Zones 5-9, dies back to the ground and regrows in colder zones per NC State) rather than a container/indoor plant, so none of the sources give indoor day/night temperature targets, chilling-injury thresholds, ambient humidity percentages, or foot-candle light figures that the schema's houseplant-oriented fields call for.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are left null: no admissible source gives a specific soil-check depth or a numeric day-interval watering schedule for this in-ground shrub; the only watering guidance found is the qualitative 'Water: Medium' / 'medium moisture' categorization from Missouri Botanical Garden and general drought-tolerance-once-established language from Clemson, which support water_regime but not a numeric estimate.

water_dry_down_target left null: no admissible source specifies how far the soil should be allowed to dry (e.g., surface only vs. deeper) beyond the qualitative water_regime classification already captured.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null: Clemson HGIC only says the plant requires 'moderate fertilization' once established, without specifying an application interval, active season, product dilution/strength fraction, or NPK/application-rate detail that could be mapped to these fields.

humidity_need left null despite NC State tagging the plant as resistant to 'Humidity' challenges: that tag describes tolerance of humid conditions/humidity stress, not a target ambient-humidity requirement level (low/average/high), so it does not cleanly resolve to the enum.

soil_ph range: NC State's structured tag gives 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' (used for soil_ph_min/max here), while Clemson HGIC's prose narrows this to 'a soil pH of 6.0 to 7.0' -- the two admissible sources do not fully agree on the upper bound; NC State's structured attribute field was used as the primary numeric value.
RHS lists the pH tolerance qualitatively as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' without numeric bounds, so it was not used for the numeric soil_ph fields but corroborates broad pH tolerance.
2026-09-02 corpus-wide quote verification: a quote that lightly paraphrased the page was replaced with the page's verbatim sentence (facts unchanged).

records.name_note: NC State's Plant Toolbox lists this species as previously known as Heuchera pulchra and Heuchera sanguinea var. pulchra. RHS's own Name Status field marks the current binomial Heuchera sanguinea as accepted ("Correct"), with no synonym flag, so the two admissible sources agree the currently accepted name is Heuchera sanguinea.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox tags this species non-toxic for cats, dogs, and horses; the tag list gives no toxic principle, plant part, or symptom detail beyond the category tags themselves.
records.cool_rest_note: In cold-winter climates the woody rootstock/crown is prone to frost heaving as the ground freezes and thaws through winter; apply a winter mulch after the ground freezes (or lift and replant a heaved crown) to protect it, and retained foliage color/evergreenness in winter depends on how severe the cold gets.
unknowns: Identification: NC State's Plant Toolbox entry for Heuchera sanguinea notes it 'is often confused with' Astilbe x arendsii, Heuchera villosa, and Pelargonium x hybridum, so gardeners should confirm species by flower/leaf detail rather than the 'coral bells' name alone.

The common name 'Coral Bells' is used broadly across the genus Heuchera and its many hybrid cultivars (e.g. 'Palace Purple', 'Caramel', 'Citronelle') in Clemson HGIC's and UGA CAES Field Report's admissible-domain articles, but those articles discuss H. americana, H. micrantha, and H. villosa parentage specifically and never name H. sanguinea, so they were deliberately not used to support any schema field here, to avoid genus-level inference onto the straight species.

water_regime: left null despite apparent care relevance because the admissible sources conflict on drought tolerance. NC State tags this species 'drought tolerant' and lists Drought and Dry Soil under Resistance To Challenges, while Missouri Botanical Garden's culture notes say 'If grown in full sun, consistent moisture is particularly important. Scorch and general foliage decline often occur if soils are allowed to dry out.' Given that tension, no single water_regime enum token could be assigned without silently picking a side the sources themselves don't agree on.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: none of the admissible sources frame watering as a container dry-down cycle for this in-ground garden perennial (only a categorical 'Water: Medium' tag and general soil-moisture language exist), so these were left null rather than invented.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: RHS's Growing Conditions field lists pH as 'Neutral' only, with no numeric range given, and NC State's Plant Toolbox page for this species carries no Soil pH attribute at all, so no numeric bound was assigned.

chill_damage_f: sources describe 'frost heaving of roots' (Missouri Botanical Garden) and a woody rootstock that 'tends to lift out of the ground' in winter (RHS) -- a soil-heave/root-exposure problem from freeze-thaw cycling, not a stated temperature at which chilling or frost damage to the plant itself begins, so no chill_damage_f value was taken from it.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives day or night air-temperature operating ranges for this species; only a winter cold-hardiness zone/rating exists (USDA 3a-8b per NC State; RHS H6, 'hardy in all of UK and northern Europe (-20 to -15)'), which is a winter survival floor, not a day/night operating range.

humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max and light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: none of the admissible sources give ambient humidity percentages or foot-candle light measurements for this outdoor garden perennial; light is described only in NC State's and RHS's qualitative full-sun/partial-shade/dappled-sunlight categories, which is why outdoor_sun_exposure is populated but the numeric light and humidity fields are not.
fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: no admissible source addresses fertilizer timing, dose, or strength for this species.

Frost heaving distinct from pest/disease: Missouri Botanical Garden's Problems section states 'No serious insect or disease problems. Frost heaving of roots may occur when winter temperatures fluctuate widely' -- a winter-care caveat worth flagging even though it isn't a disease or pest issue.

is_houseplant: no admissible source frames this plant as suited to indoor or container houseplant culture; NC State and RHS both describe it only in outdoor landscape/garden contexts (edging, ground cover, borders, rock gardens, cottage gardens, woodland edges, banks/slopes), so is_houseplant is set false on that affirmative landscape-only framing rather than left null.

records.name_note: Reclassified out of the genus Perovskia into Salvia following molecular phylogenetic work. RHS lists Salvia yangii with Name Status "Correct" and lists Perovskia atriplicifolia as a synonym with Name Status "Synonym," explicitly noting "This genus has changed from Perovskia to Salvia." NC State Extension catalogs the species under Salvia yangii, with Perovskia atriplicifolia (and Perovskia pamirica) listed as previously-used names. This record was researched under the older binomial Perovskia atriplicifolia but should be treated as the same species as any "Salvia yangii" entry to avoid an accidental duplicate.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: no admissible source (NC State, RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson HGIC, Penn State Extension, UF/IFAS, UMD Extension, UGA CAES) addresses toxicity to cats or dogs specifically for this species, so both fields are left null rather than inferred either way. (Non-admissible sources such as the ASPCA plant list describe Russian sage as non-toxic to cats and dogs, but ASPCA is not on this catalog's admissible-domain list, so that claim could not be used.)

Taxonomic identification note: NC State Extension flags Salvia yangii as commonly confused with Physostegia virginiana (obedient plant), Salvia farinacea, and Salvia splendens -- worth noting for catalog disambiguation/photo-ID purposes.

chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max: no admissible source gives an ambient growing-temperature range or a specific frost/cold damage-onset temperature for this species. Only USDA hardiness-zone survival data is given (Missouri Botanical Garden: zones 5-9; NC State: zones 5a-9b; RHS hardiness rating H5, hardy to about -15 to -10C / 5 to 14F in most of the UK even in severe winters), and a zone/hardiness rating is a survival range, not the damage-onset temperature these fields call for, so it was not mapped.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max: no admissible source states a humidity requirement or tolerance for this species; expected, since all sources frame it strictly as a hardy, drought-tolerant outdoor landscape plant rather than one evaluated for ambient humidity.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, direct_sun_hours_max: sources give only a sun-duration category (NC State: 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)'; RHS/MoBot: 'Full sun') rather than a footcandle intensity or a bounded hours range -- NC State's full-sun definition is open-ended with no stated upper bound, so no direct_sun_hours_max figure is supported.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: NC State lists all three of Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0), and Alkaline (>8.0) as acceptable, and RHS independently says 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' -- both indicate broad pH tolerance across the full spectrum rather than a bounded numeric range, so no specific min/max value could be extracted.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives an explicit watering depth-check method or a day-interval watering schedule for this species. Only qualitative descriptors were found ('Water: Dry to medium,' 'good drought tolerance,' 'occasionally dry soil,' 'performs best in dry arid conditions'), which were used to support water_regime and water_dry_down_target but do not support a numeric day-interval or check-depth estimate.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength: no admissible source discusses fertilizing this species at all (NC State's fertility/fertilization section for this plant is empty of content); all three fields left null.

is_houseplant was set to false based on the uniform outdoor-garden/landscape framing across every admissible source (NC State: USDA hardiness zones 5a-9b, landscape locations of Patio/Walkways, use 'in perennial beds, drought tolerant gardens'; RHS: hardiness rating H5 for outdoor UK planting, suggested locations include gravel gardens, cottage gardens, coastal plantings; Missouri Botanical Garden: USDA zones 5-9, 'Mass or specimen in borders'). None of the admissible sources frame it as suitable for indoor/container houseplant growing.

Invasive status: no admissible source flagged this species as invasive or weedy; NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden both describe it as having 'no serious insect or disease problems' and note only a tendency to sprawl/flop as summer progresses.
records.water_dry_down_target: Allow the soil to dry out substantially between waterings rather than staying evenly moist -- rated "Dry to medium" water need with good drought tolerance once established; sharp/well-drained soil is emphasized and wet or poorly drained soil should specifically be avoided.

records.name_note: The genus name Astilbe comes from the Greek 'a' (without) and 'stilbe' (brightness), referring to the dull leaves of some species in the genus. The specific epithet of this hybrid group, x arendsii, honors German nurseryman Georg Arends (1862-1952), who developed these hybrids in Germany in the 1920s. NC State Extension notes Astilbe x arendsii is often confused with other shade perennials, specifically Aruncus dioicus (Goat's Beard) and Heuchera sanguinea (Coral Bells, also in this catalog).
records.water_dry_down_target: Do not allow soil to dry out; maintain constant, even moisture at all times
unknowns: No admissible source addresses toxicity to cats or dogs specifically for Astilbe x arendsii, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null. (Non-admissible sources such as the ASPCA plant list report it as non-toxic to cats and dogs, but ASPCA is not on the approved domain list, so this cannot be used to set the field.)
Identification confusion: NC State Extension notes Astilbe x arendsii is often confused with Aruncus dioicus (goatsbeard) and Heuchera sanguinea (coral bells).

Soil pH: NC State tags Astilbe x arendsii as tolerant of acid (<6.0), neutral (6.0-8.0), and alkaline (>8.0) soils -- essentially the full practical gardening range -- without giving a narrower preferred numeric band, so soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max are left null rather than guessed. RHS similarly lists 'Acid or Neutral or Alkaline' with no specific range.

No admissible source gives explicit Fahrenheit day/night temperature ranges or ambient humidity percentages for this outdoor perennial (those are houseplant-style metrics). Instead, sources report USDA Hardiness Zones 3-9 (NC State: '3a, 3b, 4a, 4b, 5a, 5b, 6a, 6b, 7a, 7b, 8a, 8b, 9a, 9b'; Clemson: 'Astilbes are hardy in zones 3 to 9') and RHS gives an H7 hardiness rating (hardy in the severest European continental climates, below -20C). No chill-damage threshold or 'cool rest' dormancy temperature is stated anywhere; Clemson does note the previous year's foliage should be cut back in late winter before new growth emerges, implying ordinary winter dieback/dormancy rather than a specific cool-rest requirement, so cool_rest_note and chill_damage_f are left null.

Fertilizing: Clemson HGIC's only guidance is 'Use an all-purpose fertilizer when needed,' with no interval, active months, or dilution strength given, so fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null.

Light: NC State gives qualitative sun-exposure categories with hour ranges (full sun 6+ hours, partial shade 2-6 hours, dappled sunlight) rather than foot-candle figures, and explicitly states the plant may grow in full sun given constant moisture rather than naming a maximum tolerable sun duration -- so light_fc_min, light_fc_good, and direct_sun_hours_max are left null despite outdoor_sun_exposure being populated.

No admissible source gives a specific watering interval in days, a soil-check depth, or distinct growing-season vs. dormant-season watering frequency, so water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are left null; the qualitative guidance ('soils must not be allowed to dry out') is captured instead via water_regime and water_dry_down_target.
NC State lists 'False Spirea' and 'Hybrid Astilbe' as common names alongside 'Astilbe'; the 'false spirea' name can cause confusion since the plant is unrelated to true Spiraea species.

Clemson's care page is titled for 'Astilbe sp.' / garden astilbe broadly (the hybrids sold in nurseries, predominantly Astilbe x arendsii selections) rather than being specific to x arendsii by name, but it explicitly cross-links to NC State's Astilbe x arendsii profile as a related resource and describes the same hybrid garden astilbes, so its care guidance was treated as applicable.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note bundles six distinct factual sub-claims: (1) genus etymology from Greek 'without brightness', (2) referencing dull leaves of some species, (3) epithet honoring Georg Arends, (4) Arends bred the group 'in the 1920s', (5) parentage of A. chinensis/japonica/thunbergii/astilboides, (6) NC State's confusability note. I fetched all cited live pages. MOBOT's page does contain the Greek-etymology sentence verbatim ('Genus name comes from the Greek words a meaning without and stilbe meaning brightness in reference to the dull leaves of some species') and NC State's page independently confirms both the etymology and states 'These hybrids were developed in Germany by George Arends in the 1920s' and lists 'False Spirea' as a common name -- so sub-claims (1),(2),(4) and the 'false spirea' alias are all TRUE. But none of the 12 citation entries actually quotes any of that text: citation 3's quote only covers 'Specific epithet honors German nursery man George Arends (1862-1952)' (no Greek etymology, no decade), and no citation quote anywhere contains 'Greek', 'brightness', '1920s', or 'False Spirea'. Per this audit's own stated rule that a citation covering one part of name_note does not satisfy the field's citation requirement for other parts, four of the six sub-claims embedded in this field's prose have zero supporting citation quote in the citations array, even though the source pages that WERE cited (MOBOT and NC State) contain the exact supporting text. This is a real citation-tracing gap, not merely a factual error -- the value happens to be true but is not evidenced by the record's own citations.

records.cool_rest_note: Herbaceous perennial that dies back to the ground each year: UMD Extension states "The above-ground growth of false indigo dies with the first hard freeze and can be pruned down to the ground in late fall or early spring." New top growth re-emerges from the crown/root system the following spring.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox tags this species a "Problem for Cats." No admissible source names dogs specifically. Separately, for human poisoning, NC State rates severity Low: "Causes low toxicity only if eaten in quantity. Poisonous through ingestion. All parts are poisonous. Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea." The toxic principle is listed as baptisin and cytisine, with poisonous parts including bark, flowers, fruits, leaves, roots, sap/juice, seeds, and stems.
unknowns: direct_sun_hours_max and light_fc_min/light_fc_good: left null. NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' is the fixed generic floor NC State applies to its 'Full sun' landscape-attribute tag across many species pages, not a species-specific maximum for Baptisia australis, so it was not used as direct_sun_hours_max. No admissible source gives a foot-candle figure for this outdoor species.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max and chill_damage_f: left null. Only USDA hardiness-zone winter-survival data is available (NC State: zones 3a-9b; Missouri Botanical Garden: zone 3-9; RHS: hardiness rating H7, 'hardy in the severest European continental climates (< -20)' degrees C), which describes cold-survival tolerance, not ambient day/night temperature ranges or a specific damage-onset temperature.

humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: left null. Clemson's Baptisia genus factsheet states 'As a group, these perennials are deer resistant, heat and humidity tolerant, and drought tolerant once established' -- this is a genus-wide tolerance claim (not specific to B. australis), and 'tolerant' does not clearly resolve to one of low/average/high need. No admissible source gives a percentage figure.

water_regime and the water_* container-care fields (water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis): left null. Baptisia australis is grown in outdoor garden beds, not containers, so the keep_moist/dry_surface_between/etc. categories (built around check-before-watering container care) don't map cleanly onto garden-bed irrigation guidance. Sources also disagree on moisture framing: Missouri Botanical Garden calls water need 'Dry to medium' in 'well-drained' soil, UGA CAES calls the soil 'slightly moist to dry' with drought tolerance once established, and Clemson's species-specific line says 'well-drained but moderately moist soil' -- all pointing toward a drier/well-drained plant -- while Penn State Extension's seed library page instead instructs planting 'in moist to moist-wet soil,' a genuine outlier that was not reconciled or averaged away.

soil_ph_min: left null. NC State's only pH tag is the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' category, which states no floor. soil_ph_max was set to 6.0 from that same NC State tag. University of Maryland Extension separately states 'pH < 6.8' for this species -- a different, higher upper bound that was not folded into soil_ph_max because it conflicts with NC State's more specific categorical figure; flagged here rather than silently resolved. RHS gives only the broader qualitative 'Acid or Neutral,' with no number.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: left null. No admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule, dose, or strength for this species. UGA Cooperative Extension's Flowering Perennials for Georgia Gardens bulletin notes Baptisia australis 'is adapted to poorer, low-fertility soils,' suggesting it does not need routine feeding, but this is not a numeric schedule and was not forced into a field.

Identification confusion: NC State notes Baptisia australis 'is often confused with' the hybrid cultivar Baptisia 'Purple Smoke,' and lists Baptisia tinctoria and Lupinus as native/similar-niche alternatives. UGA CAES's field report separately explains the 'Purple Smoke' cultivar is a cross between this species and White Wild Indigo (Baptisia alba), which is the likely source of that confusion.

Weed/invasive status: NC State's Plant Toolbox lists this species under 'Problems' as 'Weedy' (alongside 'Problem for Cats' and 'Problem for Children'), though it is not formally classified as invasive by any admissible source and is otherwise treated as a desirable native perennial throughout (e.g., named NC's 1992 Wildflower of the Year).

Care caveat -- juglone sensitivity: Missouri Botanical Garden notes this species is 'Sensitive to juglone' and 'Tends to perform poorly when planted close to black walnut trees' -- a siting caveat not covered by any schema field.

toxic_to_pets is scoped to cats only: the only admissible toxicity-to-animals evidence found is NC State's 'Problem for Cats' tag. No admissible source addresses dog safety specifically for this species, so toxic_to_pets=true reflects a cat-specific finding; dog risk is simply unaddressed by the sources found, not confirmed or ruled out.
The UF/IFAS domains (edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu) were searched but returned no publication specifically covering Baptisia australis; no claims in this record are sourced from UF/IFAS.

soil_ph_max — removed on audit: Citation label contains 'soil_ph_max' and the quote 'Soil pH: Acid (<6.0)' is verbatim-accurate per live fetch of NC State. However, the VALUE is in genuine doubt: University of Maryland Extension (also an admissible, comparably authoritative source, confirmed specific to B. australis) states a different, higher figure -- 'Soil: sandy-rocky soil; tolerates clay; pH < 6.8' -- for the same species, a real ~0.8 pH-unit disagreement that would matter practically (RHS separately corroborates a broader 'Acid or Neutral' range, which is more consistent with UMD's 6.8 than NC State's stricter 6.0 cutoff). The record acknowledges this conflict only inside the soil_ph_min unknowns entry ('a different, higher upper bound that was not folded into soil_ph_max because it conflicts with NC State's more specific categorical figure') rather than nulling soil_ph_max or flagging the conflict against the field itself. This is inconsistent with how the same pipeline handled comparable magnitude disagreements elsewhere (e.g. water_regime was left null specifically because sources disagreed, rather than picking one side). No second citation independently corroborates 6.0 specifically, so this doesn't qualify for the 'another citation cleanly supports the same value' exception -- the value should be treated as unresolved/null rather than asserted as 6.0.

records.name_note: NC State Extension notes that true Helleborus orientalis is frequently confused in the trade with the more commonly sold hybrid group, Helleborus x hybridus.
records.toxicity_detail: Leaves and roots are poisonous; toxic to cats, dogs, horses, and humans if ingested (NC State rates the poison severity "low"). Reported symptoms: burning of mouth and throat, salivation, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, nervous symptoms, and depression. Toxic principle is suspected protoanemonin. The plant can also cause contact dermatitis/skin irritation from handling; RHS separately flags it as "harmful if eaten" and a "skin irritant" for both people and pets, recommending gloves when handling.
unknowns: Clemson HGIC's 'Lenten Rose' and 'Hellebore' factsheets (hgic.clemson.edu) were deliberately excluded from this record: on inspection, both explicitly describe Helleborus x hybridus (the hybrid Lenten rose complex), not true Helleborus orientalis, and the catalog's species-scoping rule bars borrowing content from a related/often-conflated taxon. This meant excluding Clemson's otherwise-detailed fertilizer guidance ('low fertilizer requirements... all-purpose slow-release fertilizer'), drought-response watering cue ('water during times of drought when the foliage droops'), and pH/drainage detail, since none of it can be confirmed to describe H. orientalis specifically rather than H. x hybridus.

outdoor_sun_exposure includes full_sun on RHS's authority (Position: 'Full sun, Partial shade') even though NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden both cap this species at partial/dappled shade to full shade with no full-sun tag; this likely reflects the UK's cooler, cloudier climate versus the hotter US sources' explicit warning that the plant is 'intolerant of bright winter sun and high temperatures.' Flagging the conflict rather than silently dropping either source.

soil_ph_max was left null: NC State's own pH tags for this species are 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' and 'Alkaline (>8.0)' with no stated upper bound on the alkaline tolerance, so only the 6.0 floor is well-defined.

No admissible source specific to Helleborus orientalis gives fertilizer interval, active months, or dilution strength, day/night temperature ranges in °F, a chill-damage threshold, ambient humidity percentage, or foot-candle light levels -- these are left null rather than inferred. As a fully cold-hardy perennial (USDA zones 4-9 per NC State; zone 4-9 per Missouri Botanical Garden; RHS hardiness H6, hardy to -20 to -15°C), it is not the kind of plant for which a 'chill damage' or 'cool rest' threshold would typically apply, unlike a tender houseplant.

No admissible source gives a quantified in-ground watering schedule (days between waterings, soil-check depth, or a distinct dormant-season watering estimate) for this species; Missouri Botanical Garden's only quantified cue is the qualitative 'Water: Medium' rating, so water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis were left null rather than estimated.

NC State separately tags this plant 'Problem for Horses' and 'Poisonous to Humans,' and the RHS page notes it can cause contact dermatitis / skin irritation from handling -- included in toxicity_detail as general context, though only the cat/dog-naming NC State language was used to set toxic_to_pets itself.

The NC Invasive Plant Council is noted (per NC State) to regard all hellebores as potentially invasive via self-seeding, though the stated threat level is 'low' -- a care caveat worth surfacing even though it doesn't map to a schema field.

name_note — removed on audit: Structural check passes (the citation labeled 'name_note: identification confusion with a related taxon' contains the field name and its quote — 'Helleborus orientalis is often confused with: Helleborus x hybridus' — is verified verbatim on the NC State page via live fetch). But the field's own prose overclaims its evidentiary basis: it states 'Multiple admissible sources note that true Helleborus orientalis is frequently confused/conflated... with... Helleborus x hybridus,' yet only ONE citation is provided for this claim (NC State), and I live-fetched both other cited sources (RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden) and confirmed neither page contains the words 'hybridus' or 'confus' anywhere — they simply don't address the mix-up. The record's own unknowns section further establishes that Clemson HGIC, which does discuss this exact species conflation, was deliberately excluded as inadmissible (and I independently verified via live fetch that Clemson's 'Lenten Rose' factsheet does describe Helleborus x hybridus, not H. orientalis — confirming the exclusion was correct, but also confirming Clemson cannot be counted as one of the 'multiple admissible sources'). So the underlying fact (the two taxa are confused in trade) is true and NC State's citation genuinely supports it, but 'multiple admissible sources' misstates how many admissible citations actually document it — it's one, not multiple.

toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail: no admissible source addresses toxicity to cats or dogs for Ajuga reptans. None of the species pages on the seven admissible domains checked (NC State Plant Toolbox, Clemson HGIC, Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, RHS, UF/IFAS EDIS publication FP026, UGA CAES Field Report) carry a poison/toxicity section for this species. Targeted searches of Penn State's 'Spring Plants that are Poisonous to Horses, Dogs, and Barn Cats' article and University of Maryland Extension's pet/poison-plant resources (including a page-by-page read of UMD Bulletin 314, '100 Poisonous Plants of Maryland,' which is alphabetized and would list Ajuga before its first actual outdoor-cultivated entry, Autumn-Crocus) turned up no Ajuga/Bugleweed entry either. Leaving both fields null rather than inferring safety or danger.

scientific_name_accepted, name_note: NC State's Plant Toolbox notes Ajuga reptans was 'Previously known as: Ajuga repens,' but per this catalog's established standard, a 'previously known as' listing of a prior synonym does not itself affirmatively state that Ajuga reptans is the current accepted name -- no admissible source contains an explicit statement of current taxonomic acceptance, so both fields are left null rather than inferred from the synonym note.

soil_ph_min: no admissible source gives a lower pH bound -- NC State's 'Acid (<6.0)' tag (the only pH tag checked on that page) has no stated floor. RHS separately states pH tolerance spans 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' in prose with no numbers, so it can't supply a bound either, and the two sources aren't reconcilable into one numeric range; only NC State's upper bound (6.0) is reported.

direct_sun_hours_max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no admissible source gives foot-candle values or a species-specific sun-hour cap. NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' is the definition of its Full Sun category, not a maximum tolerated by this species -- multiple sources (Clemson, RHS, UGA, UF/IFAS) agree it tolerates full sun given adequate moisture, so no cap applies.

day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note: no admissible source gives ambient day/night temperature targets or a chilling-damage-onset temperature. Only cold-hardiness/winter-survival data exists (NC State: USDA zones 3a-10b; RHS hardiness rating H7, 'hardy in the severest European continental climates (< -20)'), which describes winter survival floors, not the day/night ambient ranges or damage-onset threshold these fields call for, so per instructions it isn't mapped here. No source addresses a dormancy/cool-rest care period either.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity for this outdoor ground cover.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength: none of the admissible sources (Clemson, NC State, RHS, UF/IFAS, UGA) give any fertilizing guidance for Ajuga reptans -- Clemson's factsheet explicitly has no fertilizer section, and none of the others mention feeding at all.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source frames watering in terms of a soil-check depth, a dry-down target, or a watering-frequency interval; sources give only a general moisture preference ('grow in any moist soil' -- RHS; 'excellent choice for moist areas, although it will tolerate moderately dry soils' -- NC State), which is captured in water_regime instead.

Invasive/weedy status (decision-relevant, no schema field): multiple admissible sources flag this species as aggressive. NC State tags it 'Weedy' and notes it is 'Listed as invasive in other parts of the country due to its quick growth and aggressive spread' (though 'in NC, it is considered a low threat to native plant communities'); UF/IFAS EDIS FP026 states it is 'invasive and not recommended by UF/IFAS faculty'; Clemson HGIC specifically warns against using it as a lawn edge because 'small islands of green foliage will soon appear in your lawn.' This bears directly on its proposed use as a lawn/turf alternative.

Disease susceptibility (decision-relevant, no schema field): Clemson, NC State, and UGA all flag this species as prone to crown/root rot (several fungi, worse in humid, poorly-ventilated, or heavy/waterlogged soil) and root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne incognita) in sandy soils; UGA additionally lists Phomopsis dieback, Phytophthora and Pythium root rot, Rhizoctonia root/crown and web blight, and Southern blight.

Identification note (decision-relevant, no schema field): NC State also carries a separate species page for Ajuga pyramidalis, which shares the common names 'Bugleweed'/'Carpetweed' -- a possible source of confusion with Ajuga reptans (Carpet Bugleweed/Carpet Bugle) that researchers and catalog users should not conflate.

normalizations: 2026-08-23: nineteenth batch of the "blind spots" pass -- Sweetgum, Butterfly Bush, Coral Bells, Russian Sage (researched under Perovskia atriplicifolia and correctly resolved to the newer, reclassified accepted name Salvia yangii, distinct from the three already-catalogued true Salvia species -- S. splendens, S. rosmarinus, S. officinalis -- with no duplicate), Astilbe, Blue False Indigo, Lenten Rose, and Bugleweed. This batch's research and verify prompts were both updated to explicitly spell out the five strict enum fields (soil_base, soil_drainage, water_regime, humidity_need, fertilize_strength) and their exact valid tokens after b36 found free-text prose landing silently in these columns -- the fix held across all 8 records, none of which repeated the defect, confirming it was a prompt-clarity gap rather than a harder-to-fix pattern. Sweetgum is notable for a well-reasoned pair of legitimate nulls, not audit removals: soil_drainage and water_regime were both correctly left null by the researcher itself because admissible sources describe genuinely opposite-spanning tolerance (flood-prone wet river bottoms through drought resistance) that doesn't cleanly fit any single enum token, consistent with this catalog's prior treatment of Acer rubrum and Ulmus americana. Restored two audit-nulled name_note fields using the auditor's own live-fetched, verbatim-quoted evidence rather than accepting an unnecessary loss of real content: Astilbe's name_note was refuted because 4 of 6 bundled sub-claims (Greek etymology, dull-leaf reference, and the 1920s/Germany breeding detail) lacked their own matching citations even though the auditor's live fetch confirmed the exact supporting text existed on the already-cited MOBOT and NC State pages -- rewritten to drop the one sub-claim (hybrid parentage) the auditor never quoted, and two new name_note-labeled citations added using the auditor's own verbatim quotes for the rest; Lenten Rose's name_note was refuted only because its prose overclaimed 'multiple admissible sources' document the Helleborus orientalis / H. x hybridus trade confusion when live-fetching showed just one (NC State) actually does -- reworded to accurately describe single-source support, keeping the same citation and quote, which the auditor had already confirmed accurate. Left null rather than repaired: Blue False Indigo's soil_ph_max, correctly nulled on a genuine ~0.8-point disagreement between NC State (6.0) and University of Maryland (6.8), both admissible and species-specific -- a real cross-source conflict, not a citation-labeling gap, so left unresolved per this catalog's established handling of harm-adjacent numeric disagreements; and Bugleweed's scientific_name_accepted / name_note, left null because NC State's 'Previously known as: Ajuga repens' synonym note doesn't itself affirmatively state current taxonomic acceptance and no other admissible source (including RHS, which was checked for other fields on this record) was found stating one -- a conservative but defensible reading, not independently re-verified at landing since doing so would mean new research rather than reviewing evidence already in hand. toxic_to_pets confirmed clean and properly scoped across all three non-null verdicts: Coral Bells false with explicit NC State '#non-toxic for cats'/'#non-toxic for dogs' tags; Blue False Indigo true on an explicit 'Problem for Cats' tag alone (sufficient per this catalog's one-of-cats/dogs rule); Lenten Rose true with an explicit 'toxic to cats, dogs, horses, and humans' quote plus matching structured tags.
